### page_1
Geophys. J. R. astr. SOC. (1979) 59, 345-365
The palaeomagnetism of Cambro- Ordovician redbeds,
the Erquy Spilite Series and the Trt5gasteLPloumanac'h
granite complex, Armorican Massif (France and the
Channel Islands)
B. A. Duff
Department ofEarth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT,
England
Received 1979 April 9; in original form 1978 November 2
Summary. In addition to a component (A) of recent origin, two NRM com-
ponents are distinguished in the Cambro-Ordovician redbeds of the Armorican
Massif. In most sites other than those from northern Brittany the oldest (C)
is probably Silurian or early Devonian, and is mainly carried by specularite
with high blocking temperatures. This component was variably overprinted
by a Devonian or early Carboniferous component (B3) which was probably
acquired as a viscous PTRM on uplift after burial, and is carried by hematite
pigment with intermediate to high blocking temperatures. In the red succession
of Plourivo-Brehec (northern Brittany) declination scatter of two inter-
mediate to high blocking temperature components (B1 and B2) is consistent
with clockwise rotation of the bulk of Europe during the late Carboniferous,
implied independently by published European Carboniferous palaeomagnetic
data.
Stable NRM in the Erquy Spilite Series yields a palaeomagnetic pole at
344" E, 35" N (dp = 21", dm = 22"), and was probably acquired during re-
magnetization following Late Precambrian or early Cambrian folding. This is
consistent with a middle to late Cambrian age of remagnetization estimated
by comparison with other poles of known age.
A palaeomagnetic pole position at 332" E, 34" S (dp = 4", drn = 7") deter-
mined for the Hercynian Trbgastel-Ploumanac'h complex is consistent with
other middle to late Carboniferous poles from elsewhere in Europe.
1 The Armorican redbeds
1.1 INTKODUCTlON
Red shales, arkoses and grits unconformably overlie deformed Brioverian, Cadomian granite
or Pentevrian crystalline basement at the base of the Lower Palaeozoic synclinal basins of
Normandy and Brittany. These redbeds are known from stratigraphic and faunal evidence to
be Cambrian to Tremadocian in age; at Carteret in Normandy and in the Loire region of
southern Brittany the age ofthe basal redbeds is known more precisely to be Lower Cambrian
(Bigot 1925) and Tremadocian (Blake, Cavet & Lardeux 1970) respectively.

### page_4
348 B. A. Duff
Van der Voo and Bonhommet (1976) isolated similar NRM directions in redbeds near
Paimpol, northern Brittany, to those in the Devonian Hyenville redbeds of Normandy.
Recently, their studies of the Palaeozoic redbeds have been extended to other localities in
the Armorican Massif.
1.2 SAMPLING PROCEDURE
Red shales, arkoses or grits were collected at 29 sites throughout the Amorican Massif
(Table 1; Fig. 1) with the aim of improving the palaeomagnetic record of the Lower Palaeo-
zoic of Western Europe. Fourteen of the sites were located at the base of several of the
Palaeozoic basins of Brittany and Normandy, and the remaining 15 were located in the
red successions of more uncertain age in Jersey and the Cbtes-du-Nord (northern Brittany).
Most of these were collected by in situ drilling. The red shale sampled at the base of the
Rozel Conglomerate in north-eastern Jersey is probably middle Cambrian to middle Silurian
in age (e.g. Duff 1978a). Owing to the limited thickness of the exposed basal red successions
it was only possible to obtain single site collections at different localities, with drilled or
hand samples typically spread over a few metres of section.
Figure 1. Palaeomagnetic sampling localities in the redbeds at the base of the Palaeozoic basins of the
Armorican Massif. The nature of the Cambro-Ordovician succession at each locality and the likely corre-
lation of these successions across the Massif are also indicated.

Figure 2. Site mean directions of NRM for the Armorican redbeds before and after optimum thermal
cleaning. The overall mean directions are shown (stars) with their circles of 95 per cent confidence.
Closed symbols: downward directions; open symbols: upward directions (stereographic projections).
1.3 DEMAGNETIZATION STUDIES OF NRM
The in situ and dipcorrected site mean directions of total NRM for the 29 redbed sites
(Fig. 2) are downward toward the SSW with variable inclinations so that they are distri-
buted close to a vertical plane.
One specimen from each site was progressively af demagnetized in peak fields up to
160mT. The NRM of the red shales and grits from Normandy, Jersey and central and
southern Brittany generally decayed only slightly during af demagnetization and yielded
endpoints close to the direction of total NRM (Fig. 3) as expected where specular hematite
or hematite pigment is the dominant magnetic phase. In contrast, the arkoses are only
slightly pigmented and show changes of NRM direction and intensity in low peak fields
consistent with the presence of magnetite (Fig. 3 (d) and (9).
Acid leaching in conjunction with thermal demagnetization often yields information
about the multicomponent nature of redbed NRM which is not retrievable by thermal
demagnetization alone (Park 1970; Roy & Park 1974).
One or two specimens from most sites were leached in 10N HC1 following the technique
of Park (1970). Specimens were immersed in the acid for a given time, washed in water,
measured and then replaced in fresh acid. Measurements were made over a period of eight to
nine weeks and typical results are shown in Fig. 4 and Table 2. During preferential removal
of the soluble hematite pigment, the resultant NRM vector rotates from the direction of
the total NRM toward an endpoint corresponding to the NRM of the insoluble specular
hematite and magnetite fraction. This separation of the soluble and insoluble magnetic
fractions is marked by a change of specimen colour from red to drab grey or brown, and by
a levelling-off in the NRM and susceptibility decay curves (Fig. 4). Changes in direction of

Figure 3. Progressive af demagnatization of NRM in some Armorican redbed sites, with corresponding
directional changes indicated (all downward directions).
NRM on leaching are variable between sites. Endpoints are distributed from steep south-
west downward directions to shallow south or south-west downward directions (Table 2).
Two specimens from each of the 22 sites stable to af demagnetization were thermally
demagnetized in air at progressively higher temperatures with 50" C increments. Many
sites show a near linear decay of NRM and blocking temperatures are distributed from
0 to 650°C. Heating at optimum cleaning temperatures suggested by Briden's (1972) stability
index (100-200°C) removes a low blocking temperature component A, but fails to separate
two or more intermediate and hgh blocking temperature components of the remaining
NRM.
1.4 ANALYSIS OF MULTICOMPONENT NRM
The thermal, acid and af demagnetization trends suggest that two groups of redbed sites
with different types of NRM can be distinguished by the different directions of the medium
and high blocking temperature (or less soluble or higher remanent-coercivity) components of
the NRM.
Type 1 NRM is recognized in all sites except those from the Plourivo-BrChec succession
and Normandy sites MN3 and LN4, and consists generally of three components A, B3 and C.
Component A has low remanent-coercivities (< 20 mT), blocking temperatures less than
150°C and scattered steep directions. Component B3 has intermediate blocking temperatures
of 150-400 or 500°C (Fig. 5 (a)-(c)). The fraction carrying component B3 is acid soluble
in some sites (e.g. Fig. 5(g)) but not in others (Fig. 5(h)). Component C has the highest

Figure 4. Demagnetization of the NRM in some Armorican redbed sites by acid leaching in 10N HC1.
The normalized decay of susceptibility and the components removed by varying amounts of leaching
are also shown. In Fig. 4a the susceptbility curve refers to specimen 4f.
blocking temperature of up to about 600 or 650°C. The critical blocking temperature above
which only C is recorded and below which B3 and C have overlapping spectra varies between
and within type 1 sites from about 400 to 500°C. The magnetic fraction carrying
component C is resistant to acid leaching.
Demagnetization trends for type 1 sites are characteristically V shaped (e.g. Fig. 5(a) and
(b)). On thermal demagnetization the resultant NRM vector rotates toward the resultant
NRM direction (B3 + C) of the two higher blocking temperature components in a plane
containing this direction and the dinection of the total NRM (A + B3 + C). Further de-
magnetization of component B3 causes the resultant vector to rotate in the plane con-
taining B3 and C directions toward C (e.g. Fig. 5(a) and (b)). Component B3 was estimated
by the vector subtraction (B3 + C) - C for specimens in which C could be determined as an
endpoint (Tables 2 and 3). Although the presence of component C in the NRM of sites UNl ,
UN2, CF, SRl and SR3 was indicated by planar rotation of the resultant NRM vector during
demagnetization, it was not possible to isolate component C as an endpoint in these sites
owing to its very low intensity relative to noise, nor to estimate component B3 because of
overlapping spectra.
Specimens with type 2 NRM are derived from the Plourivo-BrChec succession, and
Normandy sites MN3 and LN4. Their NRM comprises three components, A as in type 1
sites, and intermediate to high (> 150°C) blocking temperature components B1 and B2.
Components B1 and B2 have overlapping spectra, but B2 is distinguished as having generally
higher blocking temperatures than 81 and a different southerly declination, although both B1
and B2 are shallowly inclined south to south-west. In some sites B2 is the more easterly
component, but in others B1 has a more easterly declination than B2. The magnetic fractions
carrying components R1 and B2 are equally prone to leaching by acid, and this results in
large oscillations in declination between B1 and B2 directions on acid demagnetization

1.5 ORIGINS OF THE VARIOUS COMPONENTS
1.5.1 Component A
The theoretical blocking temperature curves for hematite (Pullaiah et al. 1975) suggest that
magnetizations with blocking temperatures less than 15OoC can be unblocked and remag-
netized in less than a day at room temperature. Component A is probably therefore of
recent viscous origin, and this is consistent with a storage test which showed that many
specimens changed their direction and intensity of total NRM over a period of a few months.
1.5.2 Components B3, BI and B2
The maximum blocking temperatures of component B3 (in sites with type 1 NRM) of
400-5OO0C reflect the extent to which component C with higher blocking temperatures

has been overprinted by conponent B3 (Fig. 5). The blocking curves for hematite (Pullaiah
et al. 1975) imply that temperatures of about 200°C (burial metamorphic facies) over a
prolonged period (> 1 1.4yr) would have been sufficient to partially overprint component
C in type 1 sites, and for B3 to have been acquired as a viscous PTRM. Component B3
was probably therefore stabilized on uplift after acquisition during burial. In some speci-

or early Carboniferous, perhaps during the uplift associated with the Bretonic phase of the
Hercynian Orogeny.

Paheomagnetism of the Armorican Massif 351
very similar to those in rock units such as the Tr6gasteLPloumanac'h granite with middle
to late Carboniferous NRM. However, the in situ and dip-corrected directions of El and
B2 in some type 2 sites are similar because of the easterly or westerly shallow dipping
nature of the redbeds, and this suggests that the scatter, which is mainly one of declination,
originated by some process other than folding about shallowly inclined meridional axes.
Possible origins of this scatter are:
(1) Preferred orientation of DRM in the bedding plane, with an azimuthal scatter of
directions. However, it is likely that components B1 and B2 were acquired during de-
magnetization. In addition, the SSW declinations are inconsistent with the north-west to
north-east declinations in Cambrian and Ordovician igneous rocks in the Armorican Massif
(Duff 1978b).
(2) Rotation of the direction of NRM toward a horizontal, oblate magnetic fabric. The
homogeneous, finely divided nature of the hematite probably precludes large magnetic
anisotropy.
(3) Failure to separate components B1 and B2 owing, perhaps, to overlapping blocking
temperature (or 'solubility') spectra, so that the estimate of NRM directions lies in a plane
between these components. This probably only accounts for the declination scatter in a few
specimens which show declination swings during demagnetization.
(4) Local tectonic rotations in the Armorican Massif associated with the Hercynian
Orogeny, or magnetization during coherent late Carboniferous rotation of the bulk of
Europe about a vertical axis. Although variable local rotations would best explain why in
some specimens B2 is east of B1, while in others it is the more westerly component, there
is little geological evidence for differential rotations of the Cbtes-du-Nord redbeds about
vertical axes. Coherent rotations about a Euler axis in or near Europe however, is consistent
with results from the Bohemian Massif (Birkenmajer, Krs & Nairn 1968) and with Carboni-
ferous palaeomagnetic pole positions from elsewhere in Europe (Duff 1978b). It suggests
that if components B 1 and B2 have been correctly separated, they must have been acquired
at least partly during rotation to explain the great variability in their declination difference
(either in situ or dip-corrected). Coherent rotation could be consistent with the variable
easterly or westerly declination of B2 relative to B1 if these components were of variable
relative age.
1.5.3 Component C
Comparison of the maximum blocking temperatures of component C (about 600-650°C)
with the theoretical blocking curves for hematite (Pullaiah et al. 1975) implies that the
redbeds would have had to have been heated to greater than 500°C for a sustained period
(> 1 Myr) for C to have been acquired as a viscous PTRM. Since there is no evidence of
such metamorphism, component C was probably acquired as a CRM rather than a viscous
PTRM. Comparison of in situ and dip-corrected C directions determined from the end-
points of thermal and acid demagnetization implies with 95 per cent confidence (Cox 1969)
that component C was acquired before Westphalian folding. The dip-corrected mean
direction of C from seven sites, D = 228", I= 63" (16 specimens; Fig. 6), yields a palaeo-
magnetic pole at 325" E 11" N (Table 5, Fig. 7). Comparison with the European apw path
implies that component C was acquired during the Silurian or early Devonian.
1.6 CARRIERS OF NRM IN THE RED SHALE OF THE ROZEL CONGLOMERATE
To obtain further insight into the origin of the intermediate and high blocking temperature
components B3 and C, and their possible carriers, the nature of the Fe-Ti oxides and the

magnetic properties of the red shale at the base of the Rozel Conglomerate (Jersey) were
investigated.
1.6.1 Magnetic properties
The remanent-coercivity spectra (Dunlop 1972) for a specimen leached in 10N HCl and an
unleached specimen from the same sample were derived from hysteresis of IRM curves,
and are shown below the initial magnetization curves in Fig. 8. Both leached and unleached
specimens failed to saturate in fields of 1000mT. There is a marked difference, however,
in the coercivities of unsaturated remanence (HR)f;or the unleached and leached specimens
HR is S00mT and 320mT respectively. The remanent-coercivity spectra are also quite
distinctive. According to Dunlop's (1972) criteria, the spectrum of the unleached specimen
implies that the IRM is carried mainly by hematite pigment and some specularite. The
remanent-coercivity spectrum is displaced after leaching of the red pigment toward lower
values, so that the bulk of IRM resides in the range 0-600 mT (Fig. 8). This implies that the
harder IRM in the red shales is carried by the red pigment leached out by acid, and that
residual specularite probably carries the bulk of IRM in the leached specimen.
These results are consistent with high field thermomagnetic analyses and imply that
NRM in the red shale is carried by pure hematite, which is present both as pigment and
specularite. Although the pigment is magnetically harder that the specularite, thermal de-
magnetization in conjunction with acid leaching suggests that most of the pigment has lower
blocking temperatures than the specularite. Concurrence of endpoints with the component
C direction after both acid and thermal demagnetization, and the similar leaching and
thermal demagnetization trends imply that components A and B3 are carried by soluble
hematite pigment, and that the high blocking temperature component C is mainly carried
by the insoluble specularite.
1.6.2 Origin and composition of the hematite
Hematite is present in the red shales as part of the interstitial cement which binds clasts,
and as discrete specularite grains independent of the pigment. In addition, most iron silicate

Paheomagnetism of the Armorican Massif 359
clasts are partially replaced by hematite pigment. Biotite is preferentially replaced along
its cleavage, and relict amphiboles and volcanic rock fragments have distinct hematite haloes.
Only a few grains of relict detrital magnetite are observed.
These textures imply that the interstitial pigment may have been derived from the post-
depositional decomposition of former iron silicate grains during authigenesis. This is con-
sistent with the results of Walker (1967, 1974), who has shown that the formation of red
pigment in redbeds occurs during diagenesis when iron bearing detrital grains alter first to
iron hydroxides then to authigenic hematite, depending on the local interstitial Eh/Ph
environment. He cites the presence of haloes around detrital grains, as in the red shales of
the Rozel Conglomerate, as diagnostic of this process. The specularite may also have crystal-
lized during post-depositional processes (Turner & Ixer 1977). Acquisition of CRM associated
with authigenic growth of the pigment and specularite from detrital grains is consistent with
the absence of a Cambro-Ordovician DRM in the redbed sites.
1.7 MAGNETIZATIONH ISTORY OF THE ARMORICAN REDBEDS
The palaeomagnetic results from the Armorican redbeds and the more detailed studies of
the red shale from the Rozel Conglomerate suggests the following history:
(1) Clastic deposition of iron silicates, magnetites and possibly specularite during the
Cambrian or early Ordovician.
(2) Acquisition during Silurian or early Devonian times of component C, the oldest
magnetization, probably as a CFW associated with the growth of specularite and possibly
less soluble hematite pigment.
(3) Acquisition of component B3 during remagnetization of most sites other than those
in the PlouriveBrBhec succession in Devonian to early Carboniferous times. Component
B3 was probably acquired as a viscous PTRM during burial, which variably overprinted the
older component C and was stabilized on uplift - perhaps during the Bretonic phase of the
Hercynian Orogeny.
(4) Acquisition in the red successions of Plourivo-BrChec and some other sites (MN3
and LN4) of components of B1 and B2, possibly also as viscous PTRMs, during the late
Carboniferous. These have overprinted any record of older (C, B3 or other) magnetizations.
The most likely origin of the declination scatter is magnetization before, after and possibly
during the late Carboniferous rotation of Europe.
2 The Erquy Spilite Series
2.1 INTRODUCTION
The Erquy Spilite Series (Auvray 1968) crop out on the north-eastern side of the Baie de
Saint-Brieuc on the north coast of Brittany. Collections for palaeomagnetic study were
made by in situ drilling at five sites distributed through the well-exposed section on Pointe
de la Heussaye, immediately south-west of Erquy (Fig. 9). Auvray (1968) has distinguished
pillow lavas, basic sills, breccias, tuffs and sediments in this section. The controversial
Lower Ordovician age assigned to the Erquy Spilite Series by Vidal et al. (1971) and Deunff
et al. (1973) was based on microfauna and Rb-Sr whole rock results obtained from lutites,
pillow lavas and keratophyres in the section.
The asymmetry of metabasaltic pillows indicates that the entire section is overturned;
it dips very steeply southward, but ‘youngs’ northward. Two sites, CD3 and CD4, are located
in pillow metabasalt toward the northern extremity of Pointe de la Heussaye. Sites CD5,

CD6 and CD7 are located in fine-grained dolerite sills which are intercalated in the meta-
basalts, tuffs and sediments in different parts of the section toward the mainland (south-
east) end of Pointe de la Heussaye. Petrographic and geochemical studies suggest that the
sills are cogenetic with the metabasalts (Auvray 1968) and can therefore be regarded as part
of the Erquy Spilite Series. The dip of the sills was estimated from adjacent tuffs or sediments.
2.2 NKM AND AF DEMAGNETIZATION
Intensities of NRM in the metabasalts and sills are typically of the order 1O-I-1 A/m. The
five site mean directions of total NRM (in situ) are distributed about a steep overall mean
direction D = 264", I =8 1" (agg = 21"). After correction for structural dip by restoring the
sequence so that it 'youngs' upward, the five site mean directions are distributed about
D = 347", I = -So (ass= 19"; Fig. 10). Bothin situ and dipcorrected overall mean directions
of total NRM are oblique and significantly different at the 95 per cent probability level
from the direction of the present field at Erquy (D = 352", I= 65").
The NRM of at least two specimens from each site was progressively af demagnetized
in peak fields up to 100mT, and an example of the corresponding change in intensity and
direction of NRM of a specimen from four sites is shown in Fig. 11. Half of the initial NRM
is demagnetized in fields of 0-lOmT. There is a marked decrease in the decay of NRM in

specimens from the metabasalt of CD4 and the sill of CD5 over the range of peak fields
from 20 to 40mT, which reflects the separation of a soft component with low coercivities
of remanence below 20mT from a harder component of NRM. The NRM of specimens
from the other sites decayed continuously with increasing peak fields. The optimum peak
field for site cleaning, corresponding to the maximum stability indices (indicated by arrows
in Fig. 11) varied between sites according to the variation in the remanent-coercivity spectra
of the harder component of NRM.
2.3 ANALYSIS OF NRM DIRECTIONS
After demagnetization at the optimum peak fields in situ site mean directions of NRM
converged toward an overall mean direction D = 221", I = 82" (ag5= 11"; Fig. 10, Table
5). Dipcorrected site mean directions (Fig. 10) yielded an overall mean direction D = 350".
I=- 1" (ag5= 15"). A two-tier analysis of stable NRM directions (Watson & Irving 1957)
shows that the between-site scatter is significant at the 95 per cent probability level for
both in siru and dipcorrected results (F8,50= 8.5 and 17.3 respectively), and that it is
larger for the dipcorrected results.
Although the estimate of precision for the overall mean direction determined in siru
(0 = 55) is nearly twice that for the dip-corrected overall mean (0 = 28), a test of the relative
age of NRM and folding (Cox 1969) is inconclusive; there is insufficient variability in the
attitude of bedding between the five sites. However, for the following reasons a stable
magnetization in the Erquy Spilites is considered to have been most likely acquired after
folding:
(1) The Erquy Spilites were folded in the Late Precambrian or early Cambrian during
the Cadomian Orogeny. This is indicated by unconformable relationships with the Cambrian
redbeds and arkoses of Erquy and Cap FrChel.
(2) A metamorphic event overprinting the primary paragenesis occurred after this
folding, and was associated with isotopic rehomogenization of the Rb-Sr system during
the early Ordovician (Brown & Roach 1972).
It is very probably that stable NRM in the Erquy Spilites was acquired perhaps as a -
PTRM - during this post-folding event, and this interpretation is consistent with a middle
to late Cambrian age determined for the in siru magnetization by comparison of the corre-
sponding pole with the polar wander path for Europe (Duff 1978b). The palaeomagnetically
significant mean direction of NRM for the Erquy Spilites is therefore determined in siru as
D = 221", I = 82", which corresponds to a palaeomagnetic pole position at 344" E 35" N
(Table 5).
3 The TrCgastel-Ploumanac'h granite complex
3.1 INTRODUCTION
The Tregastel-Ploumanac'h granite is a high level, subvolcanic complex on the north coast of
Brittany west of Perros-Guirec (Cbtes-du-Nord). It consists of three main granite phases
(Fig. 12) that were emplaced successively, so that the youngest phase forms the core of the
complex (Barriere 1976). Features typical of high level granites such as cone sheets, ring
dykes and autobreccias are present in the outer granite phase. An Rb-Sr whole rock age
of 300 k 5 Myr (middle Carboniferous) and an incidental K-Ar biotite age (300 ? 6) indi-
cates that the complex was emplaced and cooled very rapidly (Adams 1976). Stable NRM
is therefore the most likely to have been acquired about 300Myr ago. Nine sites were

sampled in the TrCgastel-Ploumanac'h complex: three in the diorites; three in the 'inter-
mediate' granites, and three in the youngest phase, the granite of the Ile Grande (Fig. 12).
The outermost granite phase, which intrudes gneissic basement, was too coarse for palaeo-
magnetic study.

The nine site mean directions of total NRM (Fig. 10) are distributed close to a SSE trending

Only five of the nine sites were stable against af demagnetization. The unstable sites were
